system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old male with a history of kidney transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for evaluation and treatment of right renal artery stenosis, which was contributing to poorly controlled hypertension. A renal artery duplex ultrasound suggested significant narrowing, prompting an endovascular procedure. The patient underwent a successful renal arteriogram with CO2 contrast followed by placement of a non-drug-eluting stent in the right transplanted renal artery. The procedure was uncomplicated, and postoperative labs showed stable renal function. The patient was monitored for 24 hours, restarted on antihypertensives, and discharged home in stable condition with instructions for activity restrictions, wound care, and dual antiplatelet therapy. Follow-up was arranged with vascular surgery and transplant nephrology in two weeks for clinical assessment and surveillance imaging.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Hyperplasia of prostate, unspecified, without urinary obstruction and other lower urinary symptoms (LUTS)
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of bladder

Home

renal artery stenosis
 
Discharge Condition:
Mental Status: Clear and coherent.
Level of Consciousness: Alert and interactive.
Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.
 
Discharge Instructions:
Division of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery
Lower Extremity Angioplasty/Stent Discharge Instructions

Medications:
If instructed, take Aspirin 325mg (enteric coated) once daily 
If instructed, take Plavix (Clopidogrel) 75mg once daily
Continue all other medications you were taking before surgery, 
unless otherwise directed
You make take Tylenol or prescribed pain medications for any 
post procedure pain or discomfort

What to expect when you go home:
It is normal to have slight swelling of the legs:
Elevate your leg above the level of your heart (use ___ 
pillows or a recliner) every ___ hours throughout the day and at 
night
Avoid prolonged periods of standing or sitting without your 
legs elevated
It is normal to feel tired and have a decreased appetite, your 
appetite will return with time 
Drink plenty of fluids and eat small frequent meals
It is important to eat nutritious food options (high fiber, 
lean meats, vegetables/fruits, low fat, low cholesterol) to 
maintain your strength and assist in wound healing
To avoid constipation: eat a high fiber diet and use stool 
softener while taking pain medication

What activities you can and cannot do:
When you go home, you may walk and go up and down stairs
You may shower (let the soapy water run over groin incision, 
rinse and pat dry)
Your incision may be left uncovered, unless you have small 
amounts of drainage from the wound, then place a dry dressing or 
band aid over the area that is draining, as needed
No heavy lifting, pushing or pulling (greater than 5 lbs) for 
1 week (to allow groin puncture to heal)
After 1 week, you may resume sexual activity
After 1 week, gradually increase your activities and distance 
walked as you can tolerate
No driving until you are no longer taking pain medications
Call and schedule an appointment to be seen in ___ weeks for 
post procedure check and ultrasound 

What to report to office:
Numbness, coldness or pain in lower extremities 
Temperature greater than 101.5F for 24 hours
New or increased drainage from incision or white, yellow or 
green drainage from incisions
Bleeding from groin puncture site

SUDDEN, SEVERE BLEEDING OR SWELLING (Groin puncture site)
Lie down, keep leg straight and have someone apply firm 
pressure to area for 10 minutes. If bleeding stops, call 
vascular office ___. If bleeding does not stop, call 
___ for transfer to closest Emergency Room. 

 
Followup Instructions:
___

- Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

- Pure hypercholesterolemia
- Atherosclerosis of renal artery
- Hyperplasia of prostate, unspecified, without urinary obstruction and other lower urinary symptoms (LUTS)
- Surgical operation with implant of artificial internal device causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication,without mention of misadventure at time of operation
- Personal history of malignant neoplasm of other urinary organs
- Long-term (current) use of insulin

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Patel, one of the vascular surgery team. You’ve been admitted because of a narrowing in the stent that was placed in the artery to your transplanted kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I remember now. My blood pressure’s been high lately. Is that why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your ultrasound showed very high blood flow speeds in that artery—433 and 464 cm/sec—which suggests the stent is narrowing again. That’s called in-stent restenosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So, will I need another procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Tomorrow, you’ll have an angiogram to look at the artery with imaging, and we’ll likely do an angioplasty to reopen the narrowed stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I had the stent placed about a year ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a common follow-up. We use CO2 contrast, which is safer for your kidney function. You’ll also get extra fluids and medication to protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my other meds? Like my diabetes and transplant pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep taking all your regular medications, including tacrolimus and insulin. The transplant team checked your levels today—everything’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about my kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring closely. Your creatinine is 1.8 today—slightly elevated but stable. That’s expected with the stent issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the procedure—will I be asleep?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under light sedation. It’s not open surgery—just a small puncture in the groin to thread the catheter up to the kidney artery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And how long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely two days. We’ll watch you closely after the procedure, especially your blood pressure and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re getting ready for your procedure today. Any questions before we go over consent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No new questions. Just want to make sure the stent stays open this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use a balloon to reopen it. Since it’s a repeat narrowing, we won’t place another stent—just open the existing one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I’ll be on blood thinners after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll continue Plavix and aspirin to keep the stent open. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. Johnson. You’re back from the procedure. Everything went smoothly. We opened the narrowed stent, and blood flow is much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Did you see why it narrowed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common with stents, especially with underlying conditions like diabetes and high cholesterol. We’ll keep managing those to prevent it from happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure was high before—should it come down now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we expect it to improve. We’ll keep monitoring it. You’re on lisinopril and amlodipine, which help, and we’ll continue those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidney—will this help it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Better blood flow means better function. Your creatinine was 1.8 this morning—same as before—so no damage, but we’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been tired lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with high blood pressure and kidney issues. You should start feeling better as things stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ve been stable all day, and your labs look good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the groin site clean and dry. You can shower, but no heavy lifting—nothing over five pounds—for at least a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I see bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If there’s sudden swelling or bleeding, lie down, keep your leg straight, and press firmly on the site. If it doesn’t stop, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All the same. Aspirin, Plavix, your blood pressure meds, insulin, and transplant drugs. No changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vascular surgery in two weeks for an ultrasound. Transplant nephrology will also see you soon to keep monitoring your kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I feel much better knowing we caught this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Rest tonight, and we’ll get you home tomorrow. Call us if you have fever, leg pain, or any issues with the incision.

conversation_lines.text: Morning. Final check before discharge. Blood pressure is 138/76, creatinine still stable. You’re good to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll take it easy and follow the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Someone will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions. Drive safe when you’re off pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old male with a history of kidney transplantation, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for in-stent restenosis of the right transplanted renal artery, presenting with elevated blood pressure. A transplant kidney ultrasound revealed significantly increased renal artery velocities, confirming restenosis. The patient underwent an elective angioplasty of the existing renal artery stent via endovascular approach using CO2 contrast, with no complications. He remained hemodynamically stable throughout, with preserved renal function post-procedure. Pain was controlled, and he tolerated advancement of diet and activity. He was discharged home on dual antiplatelet therapy, antihypertensives, immunosuppressants, and insulin, with instructions for wound care, activity restrictions, and follow-up with vascular surgery and transplant nephrology.
